summary: ATS (ICAO Annex 11) prevent collisions, keep traffic flowing, give information and alert search and rescue. Each airspace class sets who is separated from whom. In the UK you meet ATC (Ground, Tower, Approach), AFIS ("Information", no instructions in the air) and A/G ("Radio"). Outside controlled airspace CAP 774 gives four services: Basic, Traffic, Deconfliction and Procedural; whichever you get, avoiding traffic and terrain stays your job. Know when a flight plan is required or advisable, and the 30-minute overdue rule.
sections: ICAO Annex 11: objectives of ATS
Annex 11 covers airspace, ATS units and the services needed for a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of traffic

Objectives: prevent collisions in the air; prevent collisions on the manoeuvring area (aircraft and obstructions); expedite and keep an orderly flow; give advice and information; alert search and rescue and assist it
ATS are not solely responsible for preventing collisions: pilots and vehicle drivers keep their own responsibilities
The need for ATS depends on the types of traffic, its density and the weather

ATC is provided to all IFR flights in A to E; all VFR flights in B, C and D; all Special VFR; and all aerodrome traffic at controlled aerodromes (the book lists A for VFR too, but VFR is not allowed in Class A)
Services in each airspace class
A: IFR only; all cleared; all separated
B: IFR and VFR; all cleared; all separated from each other
C: all cleared; IFR separated from IFR and VFR; VFR separated from IFR, with traffic information on other VFR
D: all cleared; IFR separated from IFR only; VFR get traffic information on all other flights; avoidance advice on request
E: only IFR needs a clearance; IFR separated from IFR; traffic information as far as practical
F: advisory service for participating IFR; G: services on request only
Trap: in Class D, VFR are not separated from anyone; they get traffic information
ATS units in the UK
ATSUs give information before flight and keep radio contact during it; control is by clearances and instructions
Area Control Centre: ATC on airways (IFR), FIS and alerting, and the Distress and Diversion service
Aerodrome ATC controls aircraft in the vicinity and all traffic on the manoeuvring area, which needs ATC's prior permission
Ground: the manoeuvring area except runways in use. Tower: the runway and the circuit. Small aerodromes: Tower does both
Approach: departing the circuit, joining, and operating nearby. Normally departures call the Tower (or Ground) first; arrivals call Approach first
In a radar-equipped CTR you get a Radar Control Service: comply with the clearance, or ask for an alternative before deviating
Non-radio aircraft: light signals (also from a runway control van) and ground signals

Near aerodromes separation may be reduced if the controller can see both aircraft, or the pilots can see each other and say they will keep their own separation, or a following pilot has the one ahead in sight
AFIS, A/G radio and Safetycom
AFIS ("Information"): at aerodromes without ATC, information for safe flight in the ATZ. No instructions to aircraft in the air; on the ground, instructions should be followed
A/G radio ("Radio"): neither ATC nor AFIS; usually staff without ATC qualifications
Safetycom 135.480 MHz: shared by airfields without their own frequency. Expect congestion; keep calls short
Use Safetycom only below 2,000 ft aal (or 1,000 ft above circuit height) and within 10 nm of your landing aerodrome
Lower Airspace Radar Service (LARS)
Outside controlled airspace up to FL100, within about 30 nm of a participating civil or military unit
Provides a Basic, Traffic or Deconfliction Service on request
Three unanswered calls: assume the unit is closed
LARS frequencies are on the 1:500,000 and 1:250,000 charts
UK Flight Information Services (CAP 774)
In Class G, the pilot is ultimately responsible for collision avoidance and terrain clearance, whatever the service
Four services: Basic, Traffic, Deconfliction, Procedural. An alerting service comes with all of them
Agreeing a service is a "contract": both sides keep to its definition
FISOs can only give a Basic Service; the others need a controller
You choose the service; the controller asks if you don't say. Units without radar give a Procedural Service to IFR procedures as routine
The controller tells you when the service is reduced (high workload or traffic, SSR only, edge of radar cover)
Instructions outside controlled airspace are not mandatory, but follow them where you can

Agreements (with a controller, not a FISO, under a Basic or Traffic Service) on route, heading, level or area: don't break one without telling the controller and getting a reply, unless safety requires it
Basic Service
Maximum autonomy: advice and information for safe and efficient flight (weather, serviceability, aerodrome conditions, aerial activity)
For IFR or VFR, but may not suit IMC
Traffic information should not be expected. Outside an ATZ there is no obligation to give it
You may be identified, but nobody is monitoring your flight
You may change heading, route or level without telling the controller, unless you have an agreement
You avoid other traffic unaided
Traffic Service
Radar-based: a Basic Service plus radar-derived traffic information
IFR or VFR. If a heading or level would take you into IMC and you are not qualified, say so
You are identified and told so
Headings and levels may be given for positioning or sequencing, but not to deconflict
Don't change an assigned heading or level without telling ATC and getting a response, unless safety requires it
Still your job to avoid traffic and terrain. Want avoiding action? Ask for a Deconfliction Service
Deconfliction Service
Radar-based: traffic information plus headings and levels aimed at deconfliction minima
Minima against unknown traffic: 5 nm laterally or 3,000 ft vertically. Between aircraft with the same controller: 3 nm and 1,000 ft (some military units 500 ft)
Minima are aimed at, not guaranteed
For IFR: expect headings or levels that may put you in IMC
Traffic avoidance is still ultimately the pilot's. Ignore an instruction and the avoidance of that aircraft is on you
Only at or above the unit's terrain safe level; below it you get a Traffic Service instead
Procedural Service
No radar: levels, radials, tracks and times that keep you apart from other aircraft taking part in the Procedural Service
Other Class G traffic need not be talking to the unit, so conflicting traffic can appear without warning
Common at aerodromes with instrument procedures but no radar. For IFR, possibly in IMC
You need not be identified; accurate position reports are essential
Traffic information is given on aircraft receiving a Basic Service from that unit, but no deconfliction advice on them
Flight plans
A flight plan is an ICAO-format ATC message and the basis for a clearance. Form CA48, or online via AFPEx. Guidance: Safety Sense 20 and AIP ENR 1.10
Booking out with the departure aerodrome is still required, and a flight plan is not PPR

Must file: all flights in Class A; all IFR in controlled airspace; all flights in controlled airspace in IMC or at night; all flights in Class B to D; destination over 40 km with MTOW over 5,700 kg; flights crossing the UK FIR boundary
VFR and Special VFR into a CTR usually use an abbreviated flight plan: the details given by radio when asking for the clearance
Advisable more than 10 nm from the coast or over sparsely populated or mountainous areas
IFR in the Open-FIR does not need one on its own
No ATSU at the destination: leave a responsible person who knows your ETA
Not arrived 30 minutes after ETA: overdue action and search and rescue begin. Close the plan on arrival
Delayed more than 60 minutes (30 if any of it is in controlled airspace): cancel and re-file
Briefing, weather and facilitation
AIS online: AIP, AICs and NOTAMs, provided by NATS for the CAA
Weather: self-briefing, mainly from the Met Office. GAMET areas: North, Central, South-West, South-East. Report severe or unforecast weather to ATC
VOLMET: VHF broadcasts of aerodrome weather. ATIS: recorded aerodrome information (separate arrival and departure ATIS at big airports)
General Aviation Report (GAR): for flights to or from the UK, including the Channel Islands, unless outbound directly to the EU (not Ireland)
Airfields: designated; non-designated with a Certificate of Agreement; others (police permission, 12 hours' notice)
Common Travel Area: GB, Channel Islands, Isle of Man, Northern Ireland, Republic of Ireland
Eurocontrol charges exempt: entirely VFR flights, flights returning to the same aerodrome, MTOW under 2,000 kg

sum.ICAO Annex 11: objectives of ATS: Prevent collisions, keep traffic flowing, give information, alert SAR.
sum.Services in each airspace class: C separates IFR from everyone; D gives VFR traffic information only; E clears IFR only.
sum.ATS units in the UK: ACC for airways; Ground, Tower and Approach at aerodromes; ask before deviating from a clearance.
sum.AFIS, A/G radio and Safetycom: Information (no air instructions), Radio (A/G), Safetycom 135.480 below 2,000 ft within 10 nm.
sum.Lower Airspace Radar Service (LARS): Up to FL100, within about 30 nm; three calls then give up.
sum.UK Flight Information Services (CAP 774): Basic, Traffic, Deconfliction, Procedural; the pilot always avoids traffic and terrain.
sum.Basic Service: Information only; no traffic information expected.
sum.Traffic Service: Radar traffic information; headings only for sequencing.
sum.Deconfliction Service: IFR; headings and levels aiming for 5 nm or 3,000 ft.
sum.Procedural Service: No radar; separates only participating aircraft.
sum.Flight plans: Required cases, booking out, 30 minutes overdue, re-file after 60 (30) minutes' delay.
sum.Briefing, weather and facilitation: AIS, Met Office, ATIS and VOLMET; GAR and designated airports.

cards.a: Prevent collisions in the air and on the manoeuvring area, expedite flow, give advice and information, alert SAR.

cards.q: Which VFR flights receive an ATC service?
cards.a: VFR in Classes B, C and D, and all Special VFR.
No: they get traffic information on all other flights.

cards.q: Class E: who needs a clearance?

cards.a: ATC on airways, FIS and alerting, Distress and Diversion.

cards.q: Can AFIS instruct an aircraft in the air?
cards.a: No: information only (instructions on the ground).
Below 2,000 ft aal (or 1,000 ft above circuit height) and within 10 nm.
Up to FL100, within about 30 nm of the unit.

cards.q: LARS: no answer after how many calls?
Who can give a Traffic Service?
Which service can a FISO give?
Traffic Service: headings given to deconflict?
cards.a: No: only for positioning or sequencing.

cards.q: Deconfliction below the terrain safe level?
cards.a: Not given: expect a Traffic Service.

cards.q: Who avoids collisions in Class G?
Does a flight plan count as PPR?
When is a flight plan advisable?
cards.a: More than 10 nm from the coast, or over sparsely populated or mountainous areas.

cards.q: Departure delayed: when must you re-file?
cards.a: Over 60 minutes (30 if in controlled airspace).

cards.q: Flight plan required for MTOW over?
cards.a: 5,700 kg with a destination over 40 km away.
Recorded aerodrome information on a dedicated frequency.
General Aviation Report for the Police and Border Force.
All-VFR flights, same aerodrome out and back, MTOW under 2,000 kg.

quiz.q: What is an alerting service?
o: A service to notify organisations of aircraft in need of search and rescue aid, and assist them
A service from the Distress and Diversion cell only
A network of civil and military radio stations
A service to notify organisations of aircraft needing navigational help
quiz.why: Alerting is about search and rescue. Navigational help is a different matter, and D&D is one provider, not the definition.

quiz.q: LARS is available outside controlled airspace:
o: Up to FL100, within about 30 nm, giving Traffic and Deconfliction Services
Up to FL80, within about 30 nm, giving Traffic and Procedural Services
Up to FL100, within about 25 nm, giving Procedural and Deconfliction Services
Up to FL80, within about 25 nm, giving Deconfliction and Traffic Services
quiz.why: FL100 and 30 nm. LARS is radar-based, so not Procedural. (Units also give a Basic Service.)

quiz.q: An aerodrome Flight Information Service provides:
o: Information useful for safe and efficient flight within the ATZ
Instructions and advice to aircraft in the ATZ
Clearances to operate within the ATZ
Information for flights in a CTR
quiz.why: AFIS is information only, in the ATZ. It cannot clear or instruct aircraft in the air.

quiz.q: You receive an ATC clearance you consider unsuitable. You should:
o: Ignore it and continue as planned
Comply even though it is unsuitable
Comply with as much as you can
quiz.why: Ask for an alternative before deviating.

quiz.q: The purpose of a Basic Service is to:
o: Provide information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flight
quiz.why: Basic is advice and information. Radar traffic information is a Traffic Service; deconfliction is a Deconfliction Service.

quiz.q: A flight plan was filed for a flight in controlled airspace and departure is delayed. After how long must a delay message be sent?
quiz.why: 30 minutes where the flight enters controlled airspace; the chapter gives 60 minutes for other flights.

quiz.q: Apart from when it is required, a flight plan is advisable when flying:
o: More than 10 nm from the coast, or over sparsely populated or mountainous areas
More than 10 km from the coast, or over sparsely populated or mountainous areas
To a destination more than 40 km away
quiz.why: 10 nautical miles, not km. 40 km is part of a mandatory case (with MTOW over 5,700 kg).

quiz.q: In Class D airspace, VFR flights:
o: Get traffic information on all other flights but are not separated
Are separated from all other flights
quiz.why: In Class D only IFR are separated from IFR. VFR get traffic information. Separation of VFR from IFR is Class C.

quiz.q: In Class C airspace, IFR flights are separated from:
o: Other IFR flights and VFR flights
quiz.why: Class C: IFR from IFR and VFR. Class D and E: IFR from IFR only.

quiz.q: In Class E airspace, an ATC clearance is needed for:
quiz.why: Class E: IFR need a clearance; VFR do not.

quiz.q: ATC provides an air traffic control service to all VFR flights in Classes:
quiz.why: VFR is not allowed in Class A, and VFR in Class E get no ATC service.

quiz.q: At an AFIS aerodrome, an aircraft in the air may receive:
o: A clearance to enter the ATZ
quiz.why: AFIS gives information to aircraft in the air; on the ground it can give instructions.

quiz.q: A station calling itself "Nottingham Radio" provides:
quiz.why: Radio = A/G; Information = AFIS; Tower, Approach, Ground = ATC.

quiz.q: Safetycom (135.480 MHz) should only be used:
o: Below 2,000 ft aal (or 1,000 ft above circuit height) and within 10 nm of the landing aerodrome
quiz.why: Below 2,000 ft aal and within 10 nm, to limit congestion on a shared frequency.

quiz.q: Which service can a FISO provide?
quiz.why: FISOs are not licensed for Traffic, Deconfliction or Procedural Services.

quiz.q: Under a Traffic Service, the controller may give headings:
o: For positioning or sequencing, not to deconflict
quiz.why: Deconfliction headings are a Deconfliction Service. Under a Traffic Service, avoidance is up to you.

quiz.q: The deconfliction minima against unknown traffic are:
quiz.why: 5 nm or 3,000 ft; between aircraft on the same controller, 3 nm and 1,000 ft.

quiz.q: Under a Deconfliction Service you decide not to follow an avoiding action instruction. Then:
o: You become responsible for avoiding that conflicting aircraft
quiz.why: Traffic avoidance is ultimately yours; ignoring the advice makes avoiding that aircraft your own task.

quiz.q: You ask to descend below the unit's terrain safe level while under a Deconfliction Service. Expect:
o: The same service, with terrain warnings
quiz.why: Deconfliction is only given at or above the terrain safe level.

quiz.q: Under a Procedural Service:
o: You are deconflicted only from other aircraft taking part in it
You are deconflicted from all traffic
quiz.why: No radar: other Class G traffic may not be talking to the unit, so conflicts can appear without warning.

quiz.q: Who is ultimately responsible for collision avoidance in Class G when receiving a Deconfliction Service?
quiz.why: In Class G the pilot is ultimately responsible for collision avoidance and terrain clearance under every service.

quiz.q: Under a Basic Service with no agreement, may you change level without telling the controller?
quiz.why: Basic allows maximum autonomy; only an agreement ties you to a level or route.

quiz.q: Normally, an arriving aircraft first contacts:
quiz.why: Arrivals call Approach first; departures call the aerodrome controller first.

quiz.q: Which flight must file a flight plan?
o: Any flight crossing the UK FIR boundary
A VFR flight in Class G over 40 km
quiz.why: Crossing the FIR boundary always needs one. IFR in the Open-FIR does not on its own; distance alone (without MTOW over 5,700 kg) does not.

quiz.q: You land somewhere other than your flight-plan destination. You must:
o: Tell your original destination (or parent ATSU) so overdue action is not started
Do nothing; the plan closes itself
Phone London Information only if it is after dark
quiz.why: Overdue action starts 30 minutes after your ETA, so tell them you have landed elsewhere.

quiz.q: Does filing a flight plan give you prior permission to land at a PPR aerodrome?
o: Only if the destination has ATC
quiz.why: PPR must be obtained separately from the aerodrome.

quiz.q: Overdue action begins if you have not arrived within:
quiz.why: 30 minutes after ETA.

quiz.q: Which flights are exempt from Eurocontrol en-route charges?
o: Flights between different aerodromes under IFR
quiz.why: Exempt: all-VFR flights, flights returning to the same aerodrome, and aircraft under 2,000 kg MTOW.

quiz.q: ATIS is:
o: Recorded aerodrome information broadcast on its own frequency
A live weather broadcast for en-route aerodromes
quiz.why: ATIS reduces load on the ATC frequency. VOLMET broadcasts weather for several aerodromes.
